summary: Analyzes OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 security following the KARP design guidelines in RFC 6518. It identifies gaps in the current authentication and keying, and notes that work on solutions is already underway. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC examines how OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 protect routing messages. It explains where their authentication and replay defenses fall short of the KARP design requirements.

how can ospf be attacked with replay
what security gaps did the ospf karp analysis identify
subtitle: A review of replay protection, keying, and neighbor identification in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

tldr.problem: The existing OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 security mechanisms do not meet all the manually keyed routing security requirements examined by KARP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares each version's authentication and replay protections with those requirements and describes security work already underway at the time.
tldr.outcome: This Informational analysis identifies gaps and solution directions; it is not a protocol update or an instruction to deploy a particular implementation.

today: RFC 6863 is an Informational analysis published in March 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its description of solution work reflects the time of publication.

sections.title: The Scope of the OSPF Review
sections.content:
RFC 6863 analyzes OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 using the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) design guidelines. It focuses on requirements for manually keyed routing security and notes that work on solutions to identified gaps was already underway when the RFC was written.

The analysis credits OSPF with packet integrity protection and support for changing cryptographic algorithms. It then examines requirements that the existing mechanisms did not fully meet, including replay protection, key handling, and identifying the neighbor associated with a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: This document checks two versions of OSPF against routing-security design requirements. It describes useful protections already present and specific gaps that remained.

sections.title: How OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Protect Packets
sections.content:
OSPFv2 can attach a message authentication code and sequence number to a packet. Its sequence number is non-decreasing, but the specification does not require an increase on every packet or define how to preserve replay state across a reboot. The authenticated data also does not include the IP header, so the source address is not protected by that computation.

OSPFv3 uses IPsec for authentication and optional confidentiality. The RFC explains that manual keying does not provide replay protection in this use, and that IPsec processing complicates packet prioritization. Both versions also use pre-shared keys directly rather than deriving separate keys for different purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv2 has a sequence number, but its rules leave gaps when packets arrive or a router restarts. OSPFv3 relies on IPsec, which the RFC says does not provide replay protection with manual keys.

sections.title: What Replay Attacks Can Do
sections.content:
A replay attack resends a captured routing packet. The RFC says replayed OSPF Hello messages can cause a neighbor relationship to fail, while replayed Database Description messages can restart database exchange and consume resources. The per-link-state-advertisement sequence number prevents an old advertisement from being installed, but does not prevent all disruption from replayed packets.

If replay state is lost after an adjacency failure or reboot, an older packet with a high sequence number may be accepted and cause legitimate packets to be rejected. OSPFv3 lacks per-packet replay protection in the mechanisms examined by this analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Replayed packets can disrupt the relationship between routers and make them repeat database work. The RFC distinguishes this disruption from installing old routing information, which a separate sequence number helps prevent.

sections.title: Security Gaps to Address
sections.content:
The gap analysis calls for protection against replay within an active neighbor relationship and after a relationship is re-established. It also identifies the need to protect neighbor identification, since replay protection depends on correctly associating state with the neighbor that sent a packet.

Other gaps include safer use of pre-shared keys and an OSPFv3 authentication option that does not require IPsec. The analysis also notes that packet-type information should be available in a stable position to support prioritization.
sections.plainLanguage: Replay protection must continue across both active and restarted neighbor relationships. The analysis also calls for secure key use, protected neighbor identity, and simpler packet prioritization.

sections.title: Solution Work Described in the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC recommends developing a common approach for both OSPF versions, based on the OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication option. The proposed improvements include sequence numbers that increase for every packet, preservation of replay state, protection of the source address, and simple key derivation.

At publication, the RFC says OSPFv3 had an authentication option meeting some of these needs, while OSPFv2 enhancements were in progress. These statements describe the work at that time and do not claim later deployment or status.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed direction was to strengthen sequence numbers, protect the sender address, and derive keys safely. The RFC reports the state of this work in March 2013.
